column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which phrase best describes the independent variable in an experiment?
column14: The result the scientist measures and records at the end of the test
column15: A condition kept the same for every group in the experiment
column16: The group that gets no treatment
column17: The one factor the scientist changes on purpose
column28: The independent variable is the one factor the scientist changes on purpose. A common mistake is picking the result that gets recorded; that is the dependent variable.
column29: Think about which factor the scientist is in charge of, not the one they wait to see.

column9: Which phrase best describes the dependent variable in an experiment?
column14: The prediction written before the test
column15: The factor that is measured to see if the change had an effect
column16: The one factor the scientist changes on purpose to see what happens
column17: A condition kept the same for every group so the test stays fair
column28: The dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect of the change. Students often mix it up with the independent variable, which is the factor the scientist changes.
column29: It "depends" on what the scientist did. Is it something you choose, or something you measure?

column9: In a controlled experiment, constants are
column14: the factors the scientist changes on purpose between groups so the effect can be measured
column15: factors kept the same in every group so they can't explain differences in the results
column16: the groups that get the treatment
column17: the measurements recorded at the end that show whether the treatment worked
column28: Constants are kept the same in every group, so the only thing left that could cause a difference is the independent variable. A common mistake is thinking constants are the things being changed.
column29: The word constant means "does not change."

column9: Researchers test whether a new mosquito repellent keeps mosquitoes from biting. Volunteers put the repellent on one arm and nothing on the other arm. Which arm is the experimental group?
column14: The arm that gets the most bites
column15: The arm with nothing on it
column16: The arm with the repellent
column17: The mosquitoes used in the test
column28: The experimental group is the one that receives the treatment, so it is the arm with the repellent. The bare arm is the control group, used for comparison.
column29: Which arm gets the thing being tested?

column9: A pet food company tests whether a new cat food makes cats' fur shinier. Which cats are the control group?
column14: Cats that keep eating their usual food
column15: Cats that eat the new food
column16: The cats with the shiniest fur at the end
column17: Cats that eat a double serving of the new food
column28: The cats on their usual food are the control group; they show what fur looks like without the new food. A common mistake is choosing the group with the best results, but the control is decided before the experiment starts.
column29: The control group shows what happens without the thing being tested.

column9: A student tests whether the amount of salt in water affects how many brine shrimp eggs hatch. What is the independent variable?
column14: The type of light over the containers
column15: The number of eggs that hatch
column16: The amount of salt in the water
column17: The size of each container
column28: The student changes the amount of salt on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The number of eggs that hatch is measured, so that is the dependent variable.
column29: What is the student changing from one container to the next?

column9: A student tests whether different types of mulch change how many weeds grow in a garden bed. What is the dependent variable?
column14: The type of mulch
column15: The amount of rain that falls
column16: The number of weeds that grow
column17: The size of each garden bed
column28: The number of weeds is what gets counted, so it is the dependent variable. The type of mulch is what the student changes (the independent variable), which is the common mix-up.
column29: What will the student count at the end to see if the mulch mattered?

column9: A student tests whether the color of a bird feeder affects how many birds visit it in a day. Which of these should be kept constant?
column14: Which feeder the student likes best
column15: The type of seed in each feeder
column16: The number of birds that visit
column17: The color of each feeder
column28: The seed should be the same in every feeder so it can't explain why birds pick one feeder over another. Feeder color is the independent variable and number of visits is the dependent variable.
column29: A constant is something that is the same for every feeder. Which choice could be the same everywhere?

column9: Comparing results to the ___ group lets a scientist tell whether the treatment actually made a difference.
column28: The control group is the baseline. Without it, you can't tell whether the treatment caused the result or whether it would have happened anyway. A common wrong answer is experimental, but that is the group being compared, not the baseline.
column29: Which group is the "normal" one that does not get the treatment?

column9: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that is often written as an ___-then statement.
column28: Hypotheses are often written as if-then statements, which makes the prediction easy to test. A common mistake is writing a hypothesis as a question instead of a prediction.
column29: The second half of the statement starts with "then." What word starts the first half?

column9: A controlled experiment usually has many constants.
column28: True. Only one factor (the independent variable) is changed, but many other factors, such as soil, pot size, light, and water, are all kept the same. A common mistake is thinking an experiment has only one constant.
column29: Picture a plant experiment. How many things besides the one being tested should stay the same?

column9: A student puts 10 pill bugs in a tray that has a damp paper towel on one side and a dry paper towel on the other. After 10 minutes she counts how many pill bugs are on each side. What is the independent variable?
column14: The size of the tray
column15: Whether the side is damp or dry
column16: The 10-minute wait
column17: The number of pill bugs on each side
column28: The student set up one damp side and one dry side, so moisture is the independent variable. The number of pill bugs on each side is what she counts (dependent variable).
column29: What is different between the two sides of the tray?

column9: A gardener tests whether planting seeds 1 cm, 3 cm, or 5 cm deep changes how many days it takes them to sprout. What is the dependent variable?
column14: The number of days until the seeds sprout
column15: The amount of water each seed gets
column16: How deep the seeds are planted
column17: The type of seed
column28: The days until sprouting are measured, so that is the dependent variable. Planting depth is changed on purpose (independent variable), and seed type and water should be constants.
column29: Look for the thing the gardener will record, not the thing the gardener sets up.

column9: A student wants to know if lemon juice keeps sliced apples from turning brown. Which apple slices are the control?
column14: Slices with nothing added
column15: Slices dipped in lemon juice
column16: The slices that turned the brownest
column17: Slices dipped in twice as much lemon juice
column28: Slices with nothing added show normal browning, so they are the control. A common mistake is picking the slices with the most extreme result; the control is set up on purpose, not chosen by its result.
column29: Which slices show what normally happens to a cut apple?

column9: A Wisconsin dairy farmer tests whether adding a new mineral to cow feed increases milk production. Half the herd gets the mineral, and half gets the usual feed. Which cows are the experimental group?
column14: The cows on the usual feed
column15: Every cow in the herd
column16: The cows that give the most milk
column17: The cows that get the mineral
column28: The cows getting the new mineral receive the treatment, so they are the experimental group. The cows on the usual feed are the control group.
column29: The experimental group gets the thing being tested.

column9: Why does a scientist keep constants the same in every group?
column14: So the experiment uses less material
column15: So the hypothesis is sure to be supported, no matter what results the groups end up with
column16: So the scientist doesn't need to measure anything and can just compare how the groups look at the end
column17: So the independent variable is the only thing that could cause a difference in the results
column28: Keeping everything else the same means any difference in results can be traced to the independent variable. Constants do not guarantee the hypothesis is right; the results can still go either way.
column29: If two groups end up different, what do you want to be able to blame?

column9: Why should a student test many radish seeds in each group instead of just one seed?
column14: More seeds mean a control group isn't needed, since every seed acts as its own comparison
column15: More seeds guarantee the hypothesis is correct
column16: More seeds change the independent variable
column17: One seed might be unusual, so more seeds give more reliable results
column28: A single seed could be damaged or unusual, so its result might not be typical. More seeds per group make the results more reliable. A larger sample does not replace the control group.
column29: What if the one seed you picked happened to be a dud?

column9: A student tests whether the brand of hand soap affects how many bacteria colonies grow on agar plates touched after hand washing. Which should be kept constant? Select all that apply.
column14: The type of agar plate
column15: The brand of hand soap
column16: The temperature of the water
column17: The number of colonies that grow
column18: The length of time hands are washed
column28: Washing time, water temperature, and the type of agar plate should all stay the same. The soap brand is the independent variable and the number of colonies is the dependent variable, so those are not constants.
column29: Cross out the factor being changed and the factor being counted. What's left?

column9: A student wonders whether crickets chirp more often when it is warmer. Which is the best testable hypothesis?
column14: Crickets like warm weather better than cold weather, so they are happier in summer.
column15: If the air temperature increases, then crickets will chirp more times per minute.
column16: Crickets are noisy insects.
column17: If crickets chirp more times per minute, then the air temperature around them will increase.
column28: The correct hypothesis changes temperature (independent) and measures chirps per minute (dependent). The reversed one has cause and effect backward: the student is changing temperature, not chirping. The others are opinions or not measurable.
column29: A good hypothesis says what you will change (if) and what you will measure (then).

column9: Hypothesis: "If honeybees are given sugar water near the hive, then the hive will make more honey." What is the dependent variable?
column14: The amount of honey the hive makes
column15: The distance to the nearest flowers
column16: The number of hives
column17: Whether sugar water is given
column28: The "then" part names what will be measured: the amount of honey. Giving sugar water is the independent variable. A common mistake is picking the "if" part.
column29: Look at the "then" part of the hypothesis.

column9: A student tests whether bread mold grows faster on bread kept in the refrigerator or bread kept on the counter. What is the independent variable?
column14: The size of each slice
column15: How much mold grows
column16: Where the bread is stored
column17: The type of bread
column28: The storage place (fridge or counter) is what the student changes, so it is the independent variable. The amount of mold is measured (dependent). Bread type and slice size should be constants.
column29: What did the student decide to make different for the two pieces of bread?

column9: A coach tests whether stretching before practice changes how far players can reach in a sit-and-reach test. What is the dependent variable?
column14: Whether the players stretch first
column15: How far the players can reach
column16: The type of shoes the players wear
column17: How long practice lasts
column28: The reach distance is measured, so it is the dependent variable. Stretching or not is what the coach changes (independent variable).
column29: What number will the coach write down for each player?

column9: A student tests whether different brands of potting soil change how tall marigolds grow. Which is a constant?
column14: The brand of potting soil
column15: The tallest marigold at the end of the experiment
column16: The height of the marigolds after four weeks
column17: The amount of water each plant gets every day
column28: Water should be the same for every plant so it doesn't affect height. Soil brand is the independent variable and height is the dependent variable, so neither is a constant.
column29: Which factor could stay exactly the same for every pot?

column9: In a test of whether brushing for 1, 2, or 3 minutes changes how much plaque is removed from teeth, the amount of plaque removed is the ___ variable.
column28: The amount of plaque removed is measured, so it is the dependent variable. The brushing time is the independent variable, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Is plaque removed something you set, or something you measure?

column9: An experiment has 4 groups of snails. One group gets plain lettuce, and the other three groups get lettuce dusted with different amounts of calcium powder. How many experimental groups are there?
column28: The plain-lettuce group is the control. The three calcium groups receive the treatment, so there are 3 experimental groups. A common mistake is counting all 4 groups.
column29: Which group is NOT getting the calcium being tested?

column9: What makes an experiment a "controlled" experiment?
column14: The scientist controls what the results will be so they match the hypothesis
column15: It has no dependent variable
column16: Only one factor is changed on purpose, and everything else is kept the same
column17: It is done in a laboratory
column28: A controlled experiment changes one independent variable and keeps the other conditions constant. It can happen anywhere, and the scientist never gets to control the results.
column29: "Controlled" is about what the scientist keeps the same, not about the answer.

column9: A student tests whether planaria (flatworms) regrow faster in cool water or room-temperature water. Which is a constant?
column14: The size of the piece cut from each worm
column15: Which worm regrows the fastest
column16: The number of days to regrow
column17: The temperature of the water
column28: Each worm piece should be the same size so size can't explain any difference. Water temperature is the independent variable and days to regrow is the dependent variable.
column29: Which factor should be identical for every worm so the test is fair?

column9: Researchers test whether a new mouthwash reduces bad breath. Which group is the control?
column14: People who use the new mouthwash once a day
column15: People who use the new mouthwash twice a day
column16: People who do not use the new mouthwash
column17: People who have the worst breath
column28: The people who do not use the mouthwash give the baseline for comparison, so they are the control. Both mouthwash groups are experimental groups.
column29: Which group shows what breath is like without the product?

column9: A student puts a balloon over the top of 4 bottles of warm water and yeast. Bottle 1 gets no sugar. Bottles 2, 3, and 4 get 5 g, 10 g, and 15 g of sugar. She measures each balloon's size after 30 minutes. Match each part of her experiment to its role.
column14: Amount of sugar :: Independent variable
column15: Size of each balloon :: Dependent variable
column16: Bottles with 5 g, 10 g, and 15 g of sugar :: Experimental groups
column17: Bottle with no sugar :: Control group
column18: Same amount of yeast and water in every bottle :: Constants
column28: The no-sugar bottle is the control. The sugar bottles are the experimental groups. Sugar is changed (independent), balloon size is measured (dependent), and the yeast and water stay the same (constants).
column29: Start with what she changes and what she measures, then find the bottle that gets none of the sugar.

column9: When graphing the results of an experiment, the independent variable usually goes on the
column14: y-axis (vertical)
column15: x-axis (horizontal)
column16: title of the graph
column17: legend (key)
column28: The independent variable goes on the x-axis and the dependent variable goes on the y-axis. Students often swap them.
column29: The dependent variable goes up and down as the independent variable changes.

column9: A student tests whether ants prefer sugar water, salt water, or plain water by counting the ants at each dish after 15 minutes. Which dish is the control?
column14: The salt water dish
column15: The dish with the most ants
column16: The plain water dish
column17: The sugar water dish
column28: Plain water has nothing added, so it is the baseline that the other dishes are compared to. The control is set up before the test, not chosen by which dish got the most ants.
column29: Which dish has nothing added to it?

column9: The control group should be measured the same way as the experimental groups.
column28: True. The control group is the comparison, so it has to be measured with the same tool, at the same times, and in the same way as the experimental groups.
column29: Can you compare two groups fairly if you measure them differently?

column9: A student tests whether soaking potato slices in water for 1, 2, or 3 hours changes their mass. What is the independent variable?
column14: How long each slice soaks
column15: The size of each slice at the start
column16: The mass of each slice
column17: The type of potato
column28: Soaking time is changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable. Mass is measured (dependent), and starting size and potato type should be constants.
column29: What is the student setting differently for each slice?

column9: A biology class tests whether cut carnations last longer in water with aspirin, water with sugar, or plain water. What is the dependent variable?
column14: The number of days the flowers stay fresh
column15: What is added to the water
column16: The type of vase
column17: The amount of water poured into each vase at the start
column28: The days the flowers stay fresh are measured, so that is the dependent variable. What is added to the water is the independent variable, and vase type and water amount are constants.
column29: What will the class keep track of each day?

column9: Which of these questions could be tested with a controlled experiment? Select all that apply.
column14: Does the temperature of milk change how fast it spoils?
column15: Does the amount of water change how fast grass seed sprouts?
column16: Do mealworms move toward dark areas?
column17: Which pizza topping tastes best?
column18: Is a golden retriever the cutest dog?
column28: Water amount, milk temperature, and dark vs. light can each be changed while you measure a result. "Cutest" and "tastes best" are opinions, so there is nothing to measure.
column29: Can you change something and measure a result? Opinions can't be measured.

column9: Scientists repeat an experiment several times, called repeated ___, to make sure the results are reliable.
column28: Each run of the experiment is a trial. Repeating trials shows whether the results are consistent or just a fluke.
column29: Each time you run the test is one ___.

column9: A scientist tests whether zebrafish embryos hatch sooner in water at 24 °C, 26 °C, or 28 °C. Which should be the same for all the embryos?
column14: The amount of water in each dish
column15: The day each embryo hatches
column16: The time it takes to hatch
column17: The water temperature
column28: The amount of water should be a constant. Water temperature is the independent variable, and hatching time (or hatching day) is the dependent variable.
column29: Each wrong choice is something the scientist changes or measures.

column9: Which pair correctly names the two kinds of groups in a controlled experiment?
column14: Constant group and variable group
column15: Hypothesis group and conclusion group
column16: Independent group and dependent group
column17: Control group and experimental group
column28: The two groups are the control group (no treatment, for comparison) and the experimental group (gets the treatment). Independent and dependent are names of variables, not groups.
column29: One group gets the treatment, and one group is for comparison.

column9: A student counts how many times a minute a person blinks while reading on a phone and while reading a printed book. What is the independent variable?
column14: Whether the person reads on a phone or a printed book
column15: The lighting in the room
column16: The length of the reading passage
column17: The number of times the person blinks during each minute of reading
column28: The reading format (phone or book) is changed, so it is the independent variable. The blinks per minute are counted (dependent). Passage length and lighting should be constants.
column29: What is the one thing that is different between the two reading sessions?

column9: Researchers test whether different amounts of compost change the number of earthworms found in garden plots. What is the dependent variable?
column14: The number of earthworms found
column15: The amount of compost added
column16: The type of soil
column17: The size of each garden plot
column28: The number of earthworms is counted, so it is the dependent variable. The amount of compost is the independent variable. Plot size and soil type should be constants.
column29: Which factor do the researchers count at the end?

column9: Which setup is a fair test of whether a heating mat makes pepper seeds sprout sooner?
column14: Two trays with the same soil, seeds, water, and light; only one tray sits on a heating mat
column15: Pepper seeds on a heating mat and squash seeds in the same soil without a mat
column16: One tray of pepper seeds on a heating mat and no second tray
column17: A tray on a heating mat by a sunny window and a tray without a mat down in a dark basement
column28: Only the heating mat differs between the two trays, so it is a fair test. The window/basement setup changes light too, the squash setup changes the seed type, and one tray alone has no control to compare to.
column29: In a fair test, only one thing should be different between the trays.

column9: Which statement is written as a hypothesis in if-then form?
column14: Red nectar was the most popular in our test, so more hummingbirds visited the red feeders.
column15: Hummingbirds visited the feeder 12 times this morning.
column16: If hummingbird feeders hold redder nectar, then more hummingbirds will visit them.
column17: Do hummingbirds like red nectar?
column28: The if-then statement is a testable prediction: it names what will be changed (nectar color) and what will be measured (visits). The others are an observation, a question, and a conclusion, which students often confuse with a hypothesis.
column29: A hypothesis is a prediction made before testing. Look for the if-then pattern.

column9: A student times how long a garden slug takes to crawl 10 cm in three trials: 42 s, 48 s, and 45 s. What is the average time? Answer in seconds.
column28: Average = (42 + 48 + 45) ÷ 3 = 135 ÷ 3 = 45 s. A common mistake is dividing by the wrong number of trials.
column29: Add the three times, then divide by the number of trials.

column9: Hypothesis: "If tadpoles are kept in warmer water, then they will turn into frogs sooner." What is the independent variable?
column14: How soon the tadpoles turn into frogs
column15: The type of food the tadpoles eat
column16: The number of tadpoles
column17: The temperature of the water
column28: The "if" part names the factor that is changed: water temperature. How soon they become frogs is in the "then" part, so it is the dependent variable.
column29: Look at the "if" part of the hypothesis.

column9: A student tests whether mosquito larvae develop faster in still water or moving water. Which should be constants? Select all that apply.
column14: The number of days until the larvae become adults
column15: Whether the water is still or moving
column16: The water temperature
column17: The amount of food given
column18: The number of larvae in each container
column28: Temperature, number of larvae, and food should be the same in every container. Still vs. moving water is the independent variable, and days to become adults is the dependent variable.
column29: Find the factor that is changed and the factor that is measured first. Everything else should stay the same.

column9: To test whether acid rain harms corn seeds, a student waters seeds with pH 4 water, pH 6 water, or plain tap water at pH 7. Which group is the control?
column14: Seeds watered with plain tap water (pH 7)
column15: Seeds watered with pH 6 water
column16: The group with the most seeds sprouted
column17: Seeds watered with pH 4 water
column28: Plain tap water is the normal condition, so those seeds are the control. The pH 4 and pH 6 groups get the acidic treatment, so they are experimental groups. The control is never picked by its results.
column29: Which water is the normal, unchanged water that the acid water is compared to?

column9: A student tests whether spinach leaf disks float sooner in water with more baking soda. She uses cups with 0%, 0.5%, 1%, and 2% baking soda. What is the job of the 0% cup?
column14: It is a constant that never changes during the experiment
column15: It is the independent variable
column16: It is the control, showing what happens with no baking soda
column17: It is the experimental group that gets the highest dose of baking soda
column28: The 0% cup gets no baking soda, so it is the control group that the other cups are compared to. A group is not a variable; the independent variable is the amount of baking soda.
column29: Which cup gets none of the thing being tested?

column9: Wisconsin cranberry growers test whether flooding a bog for 1, 2, or 3 days kills more insect pests. One section of the bog is not flooded. Every section has the same cranberry variety and size. Match each part of the experiment to its role.
column14: Number of days flooded :: Independent variable
column15: Section that is not flooded :: Control group
column16: Sections flooded for 1, 2, or 3 days :: Experimental groups
column17: Number of insect pests left alive :: Dependent variable
column18: Same cranberry variety and section size :: Constants
column28: The unflooded section is the control; the flooded sections are experimental groups. Days flooded is changed (independent), pests alive is counted (dependent), and variety and size are kept the same (constants).
column29: Find what the growers change and what they count first.

column9: Hypothesis: "If sunflower seeds are soaked in warm water before planting, then more of them will sprout." Which is the experimental group?
column14: Seeds planted without soaking
column15: Seeds soaked in warm water before planting
column16: The soil all the seeds are planted in
column17: The number of seeds that sprout
column28: The seeds soaked in warm water get the treatment, so they are the experimental group. Unsoaked seeds are the control. The number that sprout is the dependent variable, not a group.
column29: Which seeds get the treatment named in the "if" part?

column9: A student tests whether a new fish food makes guppies grow faster. She feeds 10 guppies the new food and measures them each week with a ruler. She feeds 10 other guppies regular food and estimates their size by looking at them. What is the main problem?
column14: All the guppies should eat the new food so the growth can be compared
column15: The dependent variable is measured in different ways for the two groups
column16: The experiment has no dependent variable
column17: The groups are too large, so there are too many guppies to measure each week
column28: Size is the dependent variable, and it must be measured the same way for every group. Guessing by eye for one group and using a ruler for the other makes the comparison unfair. Having a regular-food group is correct; it is the control.
column29: Compare how she gets the size of each group.

column9: A student tests whether the type of bedding (wood shavings, paper, or straw) changes how many hours pet mice sleep. Which of these is NOT a constant?
column14: The amount of food
column15: The size of each cage
column16: The room temperature
column17: The type of bedding
column28: The type of bedding is the independent variable, so it changes. Cage size, food, and room temperature should all be kept the same (constants).
column29: One choice is the factor the student changes on purpose.

column9: Biologists keep mealworms in trays at 15 °C, 20 °C, 25 °C, and 30 °C and record how many days it takes each mealworm to turn into a pupa. Which hypothesis fits this experiment?
column14: If the temperature is higher, then mealworms will become pupae in fewer days.
column15: If mealworms get more food each day, then they will become pupae in fewer days.
column16: If mealworms become pupae sooner, then the trays will get warmer.
column17: Mealworms are better at warm temperatures.
column28: The biologists change temperature and record days to pupa, so the hypothesis must have temperature in the "if" and days in the "then." The reversed one flips cause and effect, and the food one tests a different variable.
column29: The "if" part should be what the biologists change, and the "then" part should be what they record.

column9: A student tests whether the amount of water changes how well wheatgrass grows. Which of these could be measured as the dependent variable? Select all that apply.
column14: The number of seeds that sprout
column15: The mass of the grass cut at the end
column16: The height of the grass
column17: The amount of water given
column28: Height, mass, and number sprouted are all ways to measure how well the grass grew. The amount of water is the independent variable, and the type of cup should be a constant.
column29: A dependent variable is something you measure to see the effect of the water.

column9: A baker wonders whether a sourdough starter rises higher when it is fed more often. She feeds jars once, twice, or three times a day and measures how high each one rises. The number of feedings per day is the ___ variable.
column28: The baker chooses how often to feed each jar, so the number of feedings is the independent variable. How high the starter rises is the dependent variable.
column29: Is the number of feedings something she chooses or something she measures?

column9: A student tests 4 different amounts of a plant hormone, plus a control group that gets none. Each group has 8 bean plants. How many bean plants does she need in all?
column28: There are 4 experimental groups + 1 control = 5 groups. 5 × 8 = 40 plants. A common mistake is forgetting the control group and getting 32.
column29: Count every group, including the control, then multiply by the plants in each group.

column9: In a seed experiment, 18 of the 25 lima bean seeds in the control group sprouted. What percent of the control seeds sprouted? Answer in %.
column28: 18 ÷ 25 = 0.72, and 0.72 × 100 = 72%. A common mistake is dividing 25 by 18.
column29: Divide the number that sprouted by the total, then multiply by 100.

column9: Two lab groups test whether vinegar breaks down eggshells faster than water. Group 1 uses 3 eggs in each liquid. Group 2 uses 15 eggs in each liquid. Whose results are more reliable?
column14: Group 1, because using fewer eggs means fewer chances to make mistakes
column15: Group 2, because a larger sample makes one unusual egg matter less
column16: Group 1, because a small test finishes sooner
column17: They are equally reliable because both groups tested the same two liquids
column28: With 15 eggs per liquid, one odd egg has much less effect on the average, so Group 2's results are more reliable. Fewer eggs do not mean fewer mistakes; they mean each mistake counts more.
column29: Think about what happens if one egg has an unusually thin shell.

column9: A scientist tests whether a new spray that kills fungus protects ginseng plants from root rot. Which is the best control group?
column14: Corn plants sprayed with the new spray
column15: Ginseng plants grown in a different state
column16: Ginseng plants grown the same way but sprayed with plain water
column17: Ginseng plants grown the same way but sprayed with the new spray twice as often
column28: Ginseng sprayed with plain water is treated exactly like the experimental plants except for the fungus-killing spray. A different location or a different plant would add new variables.
column29: The control should match the experimental plants in every way except the thing being tested.

column9: Put the steps for running a controlled experiment in order.
column14: Set up the control and experimental groups, keeping the constants the same
column15: Analyze the data and draw a conclusion
column16: Run repeated trials and record the data
column17: Ask a testable question
column28: Question → hypothesis → set up groups and constants → run trials and record data → analyze and conclude. A common mistake is putting the conclusion before the data are analyzed.
column29: You can't record data before the groups are set up, and you can't set up groups before you know what you are testing.

column9: Hypothesis: "If hamsters are given a running wheel, then they will sleep more hours each day." Which is the control group?
column14: Hamsters with a running wheel and extra food each day
column15: Hamsters with two running wheels
column16: The hamsters that sleep the most
column17: Hamsters in the same kind of cage with no wheel
column28: Hamsters with no wheel but the same cage are the control. Two wheels is another experimental group, extra food adds a second variable, and the control is never chosen by its results.
column29: Which hamsters are treated the same except for the thing being tested?

column9: In a plant experiment, why should all the plants be the same species and about the same age?
column14: So the plants grow faster and the experiment can be finished in fewer weeks
column15: So the independent variable can change
column16: So a control group isn't needed, because all of the plants already match each other
column17: So differences between the plants themselves don't cause differences in the results
column28: Species and age are constants. If they differed, a difference in growth could come from the plants themselves instead of the independent variable. Keeping them the same does not replace a control group.
column29: If a young plant and an old plant grow differently, what would you blame?

column9: A student tests whether earthworms prefer light or dark by placing 20 worms in the middle of a tray with one half covered. Which change would make her results more reliable?
column14: Put a different kind of soil on the covered side so the worms can dig
column15: Repeat the test several times with new worms and average the results
column16: Use only 2 worms
column17: Cover both halves of the tray so the worms are all in the dark
column28: Repeating trials and averaging shows whether the result is consistent. Fewer worms make results less reliable, covering both halves removes the independent variable, and changing the soil adds a second variable.
column29: Reliable means you would get the same answer again.

column9: Question: "Does the amount of shade change how many dandelions grow in a lawn?" Which is a testable hypothesis for this question?
column14: Lawns should not have any dandelions.
column15: Dandelions are annoying weeds.
column16: If a patch of lawn gets more shade, then fewer dandelions will grow there.
column17: If more dandelions grow in a patch, then that patch of lawn will get more shade.
column28: A testable hypothesis puts shade (independent) in the "if" part and number of dandelions (dependent) in the "then" part. The reversed statement flips cause and effect, and the others are opinions.
column29: The question tells you shade is the factor being changed.

column9: Researchers test whether eating probiotic yogurt reduces the number of colds students get in one winter. Which are good choices for the design? Select all that apply.
column14: Give the probiotic group extra vitamins too
column15: Give one group probiotic yogurt and another group plain yogurt that looks and tastes the same
column16: Put the same number of students in each group
column17: Count colds the same way for both groups
column18: Let students pick which yogurt they want
column28: A look-alike plain yogurt makes a good control, equal group sizes keep the comparison fair, and counting colds the same way keeps the measurement fair. Letting students pick and adding vitamins both create differences besides the probiotic.
column29: Look for choices that keep the two groups alike except for the probiotic.

column9: A student changes how many hours a day a betta fish's tank light is on. Which would be a good dependent variable?
column14: The number of hours each day that the tank light is turned on
column15: The brand of fish food
column16: The size of the tank
column17: The number of minutes per hour the fish swims actively
column28: Minutes of active swimming is a measurable response, so it works as the dependent variable. Hours of light is the independent variable, and tank size and food brand should be constants.
column29: The dependent variable should be something about the fish that you can measure.

column9: A student feeds pet rabbits 0 g, 10 g, or 20 g of carrot treats each day and records their weight. The rabbits fed 10 g and 20 g are the ___ groups.
column28: The rabbits that get carrot treats receive the treatment, so they are the experimental groups. The 0 g rabbits are the control.
column29: Which kind of group receives the treatment being tested?

column9: A student tests three brands of sunscreen by putting each one on a UV-sensitive bead and setting the beads in the sun. One bead gets no sunscreen. Why is the bead with no sunscreen needed?
column14: It shows how dark a bead gets with no protection, so the brands can be compared to it
column15: It proves which sunscreen brand works best before any of the beads are set out in the sun
column16: It makes the experiment finish faster
column17: It is the independent variable
column28: The no-sunscreen bead is the control. It shows the color change with no protection, so you can see how much each brand reduced it. It is a group, not a variable.
column29: Without it, how would you know how much each brand helped?

column9: A student tests whether pond snails eat more romaine lettuce or iceberg lettuce. Which is the best way to measure the dependent variable?
column14: Weigh only the romaine pieces before and after 24 hours
column15: Guess which snail looks the fullest after 24 hours
column16: Measure the snails' shells
column17: Weigh each piece of lettuce before and after 24 hours
column28: Weighing each piece before and after shows exactly how much was eaten, and it is done the same way for both lettuce types. Guessing is not a measurement, and weighing only one kind gives nothing to compare.
column29: The dependent variable is how much lettuce gets eaten. How can you measure that the same way for both kinds?

column9: Which statement about a control group is correct?
column14: It is set up just like the experimental groups, except it does not get the treatment
column15: It gets a larger amount of the treatment
column16: It is the group that gives the result the scientist expects
column17: It can be kept in different conditions from the other groups, since it isn't being tested
column28: The control group must match the experimental groups in every way except the treatment. A common mistake is thinking the control doesn't need the same conditions; if it doesn't have them, the comparison is not fair.
column29: The control is a fair comparison. What does fair require?

column9: Researchers test whether blue-light glasses help teens fall asleep faster. One group wears clear glasses and another wears blue-light glasses for 2 hours before bed each night. Both groups go to bed at the same time. Match each part of the study to its role.
column14: Minutes it takes to fall asleep :: Dependent variable
column15: Type of glasses worn :: Independent variable
column16: Same bedtime and same 2 hours of wear :: Constants
column17: Teens wearing clear glasses :: Control group
column18: Teens wearing blue-light glasses :: Experimental group
column28: Clear glasses are the control and blue-light glasses are the experimental group. Glasses type is changed (independent), minutes to fall asleep is measured (dependent), and bedtime and wear time stay the same (constants).
column29: The clear glasses look like glasses but don't do the thing being tested.

column9: A student tests whether hens lay heavier eggs when their feed has extra calcium. Which set of constants is best?
column14: Same breed and age of hens, same amount of feed, same coop conditions
column15: Same egg weight for every hen
column16: Same color of feed bag only
column17: Same amount of extra calcium added to the feed for every hen in both groups
column28: Breed, age, feed amount, and coop conditions should all be the same. Calcium is the independent variable and egg weight is the dependent variable, so they can't be constants.
column29: Two choices hold the independent or dependent variable the same, which would ruin the test.

column9: Hypothesis: "If ladybugs are added to a garden bed, then there will be fewer aphids." Which result would support this hypothesis?
column14: Both kinds of beds had the same number of aphids at the end of the study
column15: Beds with ladybugs had fewer aphids than control beds without ladybugs
column16: The ladybugs also ate some lettuce leaves
column17: Beds with ladybugs had more aphids than control beds without ladybugs
column28: The hypothesis predicts fewer aphids with ladybugs, so fewer aphids than the control supports it. The same number or more aphids would not support it, and lettuce eating is not what was measured.
column29: Compare the experimental beds to the control beds.

column9: Put the steps for handling the data from an experiment in order.
column14: Make a graph of the group averages with the independent variable on the x-axis
column15: Calculate the average for each group
column16: Compare the averages to decide whether the hypothesis was supported
column17: Record the measurement from each trial in a data table
column28: Record each trial → average each group → graph the averages → compare to the hypothesis. A common mistake is graphing before calculating the averages.
column29: You need raw numbers before you can average them, and averages before you can graph them.

column9: A researcher tests whether walleye eggs hatch better on a rocky or a sandy lake bottom by placing egg trays on each kind of bottom. Which should be a constant?
column14: The number of eggs that hatch
column15: Which tray hatches first
column16: The kind of lake bottom
column17: The number of eggs on each tray
column28: Each tray should start with the same number of eggs. The kind of bottom is the independent variable, and the number that hatch is the dependent variable.
column29: Which factor can the researcher set to be the same before the test starts?

column9: Which experiment is designed best to test whether rinsing strawberries in vinegar slows mold growth?
column14: Rinse 20 strawberries in vinegar and compare them to nothing
column15: Rinse 20 strawberries in vinegar and keep them in the fridge, and leave 20 unrinsed strawberries on the counter
column16: Rinse 1 strawberry in vinegar and 1 in plain water
column17: Rinse 20 strawberries in vinegar and 20 in plain water, store all of them in identical containers in the fridge, and check them daily for mold
column28: The best plan has a plain-water control, a large sample, and the same storage for both groups. The fridge/counter plan changes temperature too, 1 strawberry each is too small, and no comparison group means no control.
column29: Look for the plan with a control group, many strawberries, and only one difference.

column9: A scientist tests whether mice find food in a maze faster after eating a high-sugar snack. Group 1 eats a high-sugar snack, Group 2 eats a no-sugar snack of the same size, and Group 3 eats nothing. Which group is the best control for testing the sugar?
column14: Group 3, because getting nothing at all is always the best control group
column15: Group 1, because it gets the most sugar
column16: None, because all three groups are experimental groups
column17: Group 2, because its snack is the same as Group 1's except for the sugar
column28: Group 2 eats the same-sized snack without sugar, so the only difference from Group 1 is the sugar. Group 3 differs in two ways (no food at all and no sugar), so a difference could come from simply eating. The common mistake is assuming "nothing" is always the best control.
column29: The best control matches the experimental group in every way except the one thing being tested.

column9: A student tests whether an air bubbler helps pond snails lay more eggs. Tank A has a bubbler and 10 snails. Tank B has no bubbler and 4 snails. After a month, Tank A has more eggs. What is the biggest flaw?
column14: Counting eggs is not a good dependent variable
column15: The tanks started with different numbers of snails, so more parents could explain the extra eggs
column16: Tank B should also have had a bubbler running all month, so both tanks had the same amount of air
column17: The bubbler should be a constant
column28: The number of snails should be a constant. Tank A had more than twice as many snails, so the extra eggs could come from that rather than the bubbler. The bubbler is the independent variable, so it should differ.
column29: Besides the bubbler, what else is different between the tanks?

column9: Researchers test whether the scent of a predator makes minnows hide. They add water from a tank that held a pike to some minnow tanks. To the other tanks, they add the same amount of plain tank water. Why do they add plain water to the control tanks instead of adding nothing?
column14: Because plain water is the independent variable
column15: So the only difference between the groups is the pike scent, not the act of adding water
column16: To make the control minnows hide more
column17: So the control tanks also get some pike scent, but a much weaker amount than the other tanks
column28: Pouring water could disturb the fish, so the control tanks get the same pour without the scent. Then any difference in hiding can be blamed on the pike scent. Plain water is part of the control setup, not the independent variable.
column29: Could pouring water into a tank startle the minnows by itself?

column9: In a study of whether a new pill reduces headaches, the control group gets a sugar pill that looks exactly like the real pill, and no one in either group is told which pill they got. Why?
column14: So the control group also gets the medicine, just in a smaller dose that is easier to hide
column15: Because sugar pills reduce headaches better than medicine
column16: So expectations affect both groups the same way, and the only difference is the medicine
column17: So the study can use fewer people
column28: People who think they are treated may feel better just from expecting to. A look-alike pill and not telling anyone keep expectations the same in both groups, so the medicine is the only difference. The sugar pill has no medicine in it.
column29: If people knew they got the real pill, could just believing it work change how they feel?

column9: A student plans to test whether the amount of dish soap in water affects how tall grass grows. Her plan: "Four pots get water with 0, 5, 10, or 20 drops of soap. Each pot gets the same soil and the same grass seed. The 0-drop pot sits by the heater, and the others sit by the window. I'll water each pot with whatever is left in my water bottle. After 2 weeks I'll measure the tallest blade in each pot." Which are flaws in her plan? Select all that apply.
column14: Every pot uses the same kind of grass seed
column15: The 0-drop pot is in a different spot than the others
column16: There is only one pot for each amount of soap
column17: The amount of water each pot gets is not kept the same
column18: The pots get different amounts of soap
column28: Location and water amount both differ between pots, so they are uncontrolled variables, and one pot per group is too small a sample. Different amounts of soap is the independent variable, and the same seed is a good constant.
column29: Find anything besides the soap that could differ between pots, and think about sample size.

column9: A student wants to test whether earthworms speed up how fast fallen leaves break down. Which design is best?
column14: Set up 10 bins, all with worms, and weigh the leaves left after 4 weeks
column15: Set up 10 identical bins with the same soil, leaves, and moisture; add 20 earthworms to 5 bins and none to the other 5; weigh the leaves left after 4 weeks
column16: Set up 5 bins with worms and 5 bins without worms, but give the no-worm bins extra leaves to make it fair
column17: Set up one bin with worms in the garage and one bin without worms in the basement
column28: The best design has a control (no worms), five bins per group, and identical soil, leaves, and moisture. The garage/basement plan changes location too, the all-worms plan has no control, and adding extra leaves changes a constant.
column29: The best design has a control, several bins per group, and only one difference between groups.

column9: Biologists test how water temperature affects how fast trout eggs develop. The stream the trout come from is normally 10 °C. They use tanks at 6 °C, 10 °C, and 14 °C. Which tank is the control?
column14: The 14 °C tank, because it is the warmest
column15: The 6 °C tank, because it is the coldest
column16: All three tanks, because each one holds water at a set temperature
column17: The 10 °C tank, because it matches the normal stream conditions
column28: There is no "no temperature" tank, so the control is the normal condition: 10 °C, like the trout's stream. The colder and warmer tanks are experimental groups. A common mistake is thinking the lowest value is always the control.
column29: When you can't have "zero" of something, the control is the normal condition.

column9: A student notices that classmates who drink more water seem to get fewer headaches. Which plan is a controlled experiment that tests this?
column14: Have every volunteer drink 8 cups a day and count their headaches
column15: Randomly split volunteers into two similar groups; one drinks 8 cups of water a day and the other drinks their usual amount; both record headaches for 3 weeks
column16: Survey 50 classmates about how much water they drink and how many headaches they get
column17: Ask the students with the fewest headaches how much water they drink
column28: Only the random-split plan changes the independent variable on purpose and compares to a control group. The survey and asking students only observe, so other factors could explain the pattern, and the all-8-cups plan has no control.
column29: In an experiment, the scientist changes something. Which plan has the scientist decide who drinks more?

column9: Control-group radish seedlings grew 4.0 cm, 4.4 cm, and 4.2 cm. Seedlings watered with diluted coffee grew 5.1 cm, 4.9 cm, and 5.3 cm. On average, how many centimeters taller were the coffee-watered seedlings? Answer in cm.
column28: Control average = (4.0 + 4.4 + 4.2) ÷ 3 = 4.2 cm. Coffee average = (5.1 + 4.9 + 5.3) ÷ 3 = 5.1 cm. 5.1 − 4.2 = 0.9 cm. A common mistake is comparing just one seedling from each group.
column29: Find the average of each group first, then subtract.

column9: A student tests whether mosquitoes are more attracted to dark clothing. She hangs a black shirt in a shady spot by a pond and a white shirt in a sunny spot by the driveway, then counts the mosquitoes that land on each. What is the biggest problem?
column14: Shirt color should have been a constant
column15: Counting mosquitoes is not a measurement
column16: The shirts are in different places, so the location could explain the difference
column17: She should have counted mosquitoes on only one shirt so the counting would be more careful
column28: Shirt color is the independent variable, but location (shade by a pond vs. sun by a driveway) also changed. Mosquitoes are more common near water, so location could cause the difference. Both shirts should hang side by side.
column29: Besides color, what else is different about the two shirts?

column9: A student's hypothesis is: "If pea plants get more hours of light each day, then they will produce more pea pods." In her experiment, every plant gets 12 hours of light, but each group gets a different amount of water. What is wrong?
column14: Nothing is wrong, because light and water are both constants in her experiment
column15: Her experiment changes water, not light, so it doesn't test her hypothesis
column16: She should give all the plants no light at all so that light can't affect the pods
column17: Her hypothesis has no dependent variable
column28: The hypothesis says light is the independent variable, but she kept light constant and changed water. Her experiment tests a different question. The hypothesis does have a dependent variable: the number of pea pods.
column29: Compare the "if" part of the hypothesis to what she actually changed.

column9: A student tests whether a garlic spray keeps deer from eating hostas. She sprays 2 hostas near the woods and leaves 1 hosta by the house unsprayed. After a month she checks for bite marks. Which changes would improve her experiment? Select all that apply.
column14: Spray the unsprayed hosta with garlic too
column15: Put the sprayed and unsprayed hostas in the same area
column16: Use the same number of hostas in each group
column17: Use many more hostas in each group
column18: Use a different kind of plant for the unsprayed group
column28: More plants, equal group sizes, and the same location all make the comparison fairer. Spraying the control would remove the control group, and using a different plant adds a new variable.
column29: Look for changes that make the groups bigger, equal, and alike except for the spray.

column9: A data table has two columns: "Minutes of UV light exposure" (0, 5, 10, 15) and "Number of yeast colonies that grow." Which statement is correct?
column14: Minutes of UV is the dependent variable because it was measured with a timer
column15: Both columns are constants
column16: Minutes of UV exposure is the independent variable, and the 0-minute plate is the control
column17: Number of colonies is the independent variable, and minutes of UV is the dependent variable
column28: The scientist chose the exposure times, so minutes of UV is the independent variable, and the 0-minute plate gets no UV, so it is the control. A common mistake is calling something dependent just because a tool, like a timer, was used.
column29: Which column was set by the scientist before the results came in?

column9: A scientist tests how chlorine affects algae growth. Why would she test 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 drops of chlorine instead of only 0 and 4 drops?
column14: More levels mean she doesn't need a control group, since the 1-drop cup can be compared to the others
column15: More levels mean she needs fewer constants
column16: Several levels show how algae respond as chlorine increases, not just whether there is a difference
column17: More levels let the dependent variable change too
column28: Testing several amounts shows the shape of the effect, like whether growth drops a little at a time or all at once. She still needs the 0-drop control and the same constants.
column29: With only two groups, could you tell whether 1 or 2 drops does anything?

column9: Match each flaw in an experiment to the fix that solves it.
column14: Two factors changed at the same time :: Change only the independent variable and keep everything else the same
column15: Groups measured in different ways :: Measure every group with the same tool and method
column16: No group to compare the results to :: Add a control group that does not get the treatment
column17: Only one plant in each group :: Use many plants in each group and repeat the trials
column28: Small samples are fixed with more plants and trials. Two changing factors are fixed by changing only one. A missing comparison is fixed with a control group. Unfair measuring is fixed by measuring every group the same way.
column29: Match each problem to the fix that removes exactly that problem.

column9: A student tests whether adding yeast to banana slices changes how many eggs fruit flies lay. Which list correctly identifies the parts of her experiment?
column14: IV: number of flies in each jar. DV: number of eggs laid. Constant: banana slice size. Control: jars with banana and yeast.
column15: IV: whether yeast is added. DV: number of eggs laid. Constant: whether yeast is added. Control: jars with the most eggs.
column16: IV: number of eggs laid. DV: whether yeast is added. Constant: number of flies in each jar. Control: jars with banana and no yeast.
column17: IV: whether yeast is added. DV: number of eggs laid. Constant: number of flies in each jar. Control: jars with banana and no yeast.
column28: The student changes whether yeast is added (IV) and counts eggs (DV). The number of flies stays the same (constant), and banana with no yeast is the control. The other lists swap IV and DV, make the IV a constant, or give yeast to the control.
column29: Check each part one at a time: what is changed, what is counted, what stays the same, and which jars get no yeast?

column9: A student tests whether vitamin water helps houseflies live longer. 50 flies get vitamin water and 50 get tap water. The vitamin-water flies live 2 days longer on average. Later she realizes the vitamin-water jars were cleaned every day and the tap-water jars were not. Which statement is most accurate?
column14: Cleaning doesn't matter because it isn't the independent variable
column15: The vitamin water clearly works, because 50 flies per group is a large enough sample to be sure
column16: The result can't be credited to the vitamin water, because cleaning was not kept constant
column17: The tap-water flies were the experimental group
column28: Cleaning the jars could help flies live longer, so it should have been a constant. Because it differed, she can't tell whether the vitamin water or the cleaning caused the result. A large sample does not fix an uncontrolled variable.
column29: Does a big sample fix a problem with constants?

column9: Which of these is NOT a controlled experiment?
column14: A scientist records the heights of trees in five different forests and compares them
column15: A scientist keeps identical fish tanks at different pH levels and counts how many snails survive
column16: A scientist grows identical trays of moss under 2, 4, or 6 hours of mist a day and measures growth
column17: A scientist gives half of a group of rats a new diet and half the normal diet, then compares their weights
column28: Recording tree heights in different forests is an observation; the scientist doesn't change anything, and the forests differ in many ways. The other three each change one independent variable on purpose and keep other conditions the same.
column29: In a controlled experiment, the scientist changes something on purpose.

column9: A student tests 3 brands of hamster food plus a control group on the usual food. She puts 4 hamsters in each group and runs the whole experiment twice, using new hamsters the second time. How many hamsters does she need in total?
column28: 3 brands + 1 control = 4 groups. 4 groups × 4 hamsters = 16 hamsters per run. 16 × 2 runs = 32 hamsters. Common mistakes are leaving out the control (24) or forgetting the second run (16).
column29: Count the groups (don't forget the control), multiply by hamsters per group, then by the number of runs.

column9: A student tested whether warm water makes seeds sprout faster. In one trial with 2 seeds per group, the warm-water seeds sprouted in 3 days and the room-temperature seeds in 5 days. What is the best next step?
column14: Conclude that warm water always makes seeds sprout faster, since the warm seeds sprouted 2 days sooner
column15: Remove the room-temperature group because it was slower
column16: Repeat the experiment with many more seeds per group and several trials before drawing a conclusion
column17: Change the independent variable to light to get a more interesting result
column28: With 2 seeds and one trial, the result could easily be chance. More seeds and repeated trials would show whether it holds up. Dropping the room-temperature group would remove the control.
column29: How confident can you be from just 2 seeds and 1 trial?

column9: A student plans to test how the amount of light affects Elodea, a water plant. Equal-length sprigs sit in tubes of 22 °C water. Lamps with 25-watt, 60-watt, and 100-watt bulbs are each placed 15 cm from a tube, and the student counts oxygen bubbles for 5 minutes. Which list gives a constant, the independent variable, and the dependent variable, in that order?
column14: Number of bubbles; bulb wattage; 22 °C water
column15: 22 °C water; number of bubbles; bulb wattage
column16: Bulb wattage; 15 cm distance; number of bubbles
column17: 15 cm distance; bulb wattage; number of bubbles
column28: The 15 cm distance is the same for every tube (constant), the bulb wattage is changed on purpose (independent), and the bubbles are counted (dependent). Water temperature is also a constant, not the dependent variable.
column29: Check each item: is it the same for every tube, changed on purpose, or counted?

column9: A scientist finds that frogs in a pond near farm fields have more leg deformities than frogs in a forest pond. She thinks a farm chemical is the cause. Which experiment would best test this?
column14: Move frogs from the forest pond into the farm pond
column15: Count deformed frogs in ten more ponds near farm fields
column16: Raise tadpoles from the same batch of eggs in identical tanks; add the farm chemical to half the tanks and plain water to the rest; count leg deformities
column17: Raise tadpoles in water taken from the farm pond and water taken from the forest pond
column28: Only the identical-tank plan changes just one variable, the chemical, with a plain-water control. Pond water from two places differs in many ways (temperature, other chemicals, parasites), and counting more ponds is still only observation.
column29: The two ponds differ in many ways. Which plan changes ONLY the chemical?

column9: A study tests whether hours of daylight (8, 12, or 16 hours a day) change how many eggs chickens lay. The chickens normally get 12 hours of daylight. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column14: The 12-hour group can serve as the control
column15: Number of eggs laid is the dependent variable
column16: The chickens' feed should be different in each group
column17: There are three independent variables because there are three groups
column18: Hours of daylight is the independent variable
column28: Daylight hours are changed (independent), eggs are counted (dependent), and 12 hours is the normal condition, so that group is the control. Feed should be a constant. Three groups are three levels of one independent variable, not three variables.
column29: Several groups can all be levels of one independent variable.

column9: A student tests whether rinsing lettuce for 10, 20, or 30 seconds removes soil bacteria. She does not include any unrinsed lettuce. What can she NOT conclude?
column14: Whether rinsing at all removes more bacteria than not rinsing
column15: Which rinse time left the fewest bacteria
column16: Whether 30 seconds removes more bacteria than 10 seconds
column17: Whether her bacteria counts went up or down with longer rinses
column28: Without an unrinsed control, she can compare rinse times to each other but can't tell how much any rinsing helps compared to none. A common mistake is thinking a set of experimental groups is enough without a baseline.
column29: Without unrinsed lettuce, what baseline is missing?

column9: Which plan correctly tests the hypothesis "If students take a 5-minute walk before a memory test, then they will remember more words"?
column14: Have all 40 students walk for 5 minutes, then give the word test and average the scores
column15: Randomly split 40 students into two groups; one walks for 5 minutes and the other sits for 5 minutes; both take the same word test in the same room; compare the average scores
column16: Have one student walk on Monday and sit on Tuesday, using a different word list each day
column17: Let 20 students who want to walk do so in the morning and test the 20 who prefer to sit in the afternoon
column28: The random-split plan has a control (sitting), random groups, and the same test and room for both. The all-walk plan has no control, the choose-your-group plan changes time of day and lets students pick, and the one-student plan is too small and changes the word list.
column29: Look for a control group, a fair way to make the groups, and the same test conditions.
